claims.text: Increasing the number of constituents in a magnetic high-entropy alloy increases its coercive field.
Increasing the number of alloy constituents increases configurational entropy.
Increased configurational entropy stabilizes disordered solid-solution phases.
Increasing the number of constituents stabilizes solid solutions relative to ordered intermetallic phases.
Increasing the number of constituents reduces the formation of intermetallic compounds.
Solid-solution stabilization and reduced intermetallic formation cause an increase in coercive field.
The starting magnetic high-entropy alloy has a single-phase solid-solution structure.
The number of constituents is increased while the overall alloy composition remains constant.
The coercive field increases as the number of constituents increases.
The comparison baseline is a single-phase solid-solution alloy with fewer constituents.
Alloy composition and processing conditions are held constant during the comparison.
The exact relationship between constituent count and coercive field is not well established.
The proposed explanation does not account for possible effects of lattice strain and grain size on coercivity.
Failure of coercive field to increase with constituent count would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Increasing the number of chemical constituents necessarily changes the compositional specification, so it is not coherent to require both a changed constituent count and an unchanged overall composition without defining a substitution or composition-matching scheme.
The same two records are designated simultaneously as supporting and conflicting evidence, with no explanation of which claims they support and which they conflict with.
